question: Lower eyelid retractor repair (reattachment) is most appropriate for correction of what condition?
explanation: The lower lid retractor muscles include the capsulopalpebral fascia and the inferior tarsal muscle. Reinsertion of the lower lid retractors is performed to repair involutional entropion. In addition to reinsertion of the lower lid retractors, partial myectomy of the preseptal orbicularis oculi muscle can be performed, as well as tightening of the lower lid by a lateral tarsal strip. These procedures address the 3 principal mechanisms behind involutional entropion: 1) horizontal laxity of the eyelid, 2) disinsertion or atrophy of the lower lid retractor complex, or 3) overriding preseptal orbicularis oculi muscle. In contrast, cicatricial entropion repair requires addressing the underlying problem (eg, controlling inﬂammation, autoimmune reaction, infection, or trauma) and using a graft to lengthen the posterior lamella.

question: A patient presents with left eye pain and swelling for 1 week, as shown. Computed tomography (CT) shows left proptosis with enlargement of extraocular muscles with involvement of the tendons. There is no sinusitis. Thyroid studies are normal. What is the best next step in management?
explanation: This is nonspeciﬁc orbital inﬂammation (also termed idiopathic orbital inﬂammation). Onset is acute and painful. The pathogenesis appears to be immune-mediated. Signs include extraocular muscle restriction, proptosis, conjunctival inﬂammation, chemosis, and eyelid erythema and edema. On CT, up to 50% of cases show thickening of the BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient who previously underwent a medial orbitotomy for a cavernous hemangioma presents with a complaint of epiphora. What structure is most likely to have been damaged during the surgical procedure?
explanation: When dissecting in the medial orbit, the surgeon must be careful to avoid damaging the medial canthal tendon, lacrimal canaliculi and sac, trochlea, superior oblique tendon and muscle, and inferior oblique muscle, as well as the sensory nerves and vessels along the medial aspect of the superior orbital rim. &

question: What abnormality is characteristic for cicatricial ectropion of the lower eyelid?
explanation: Anterior lamellar deﬁciency is a hallmark of cicatricial ectropion. Lower eyelid laxity is a common pathologic change seen in patients with involutional ectropion. This laxity can involve the medial or lateral canthal tendon or both. Lower eyelid retractor disinsertion may also be a component of involutional ectropion and is typically manifested by tarsal ectropion, in which the palpebral conjunctival surface is outwardly rotated.

question: Following eyelid surgery, a patient develops an acute postoperative orbital hemorrhage with visual loss. What is the appropriate management of care in this setting?

options.D: evacuation of the clot after reopening the incision

explanation: Vision loss in the clinical scenario described is secondary to a compressive eﬀect from the orbital hemorrhage. Therefore, evacuation of the clot after reopening the incision is the appropriate next step. Intravenous steroids can be given to minimize edema; however, surgical intervention is the ﬁrst step and more appropriate. Intravenous mannitol, acetazolamide, timolol, and anterior chamber paracentesis are all treatment modalities for nonhemorrhagic scenarios.

question: What kind of assessment can help to rule out pseudoepiphora?
explanation: In the evaluation of epiphora, the initial step is to distinguish patients with hypersecretion from those with lacrimal drainage obstruction. The evaluation of pseudoepiphora involves the assessment of the tear meniscus, the tear breakup time, and the ocular surface. The tear breakup time helps to evaluate the mucin layer of the tears. This is best BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: An anophthalmic patient stopped wearing his 15-year-old prosthesis for 2 years. He has now tried to starting wearing it again, but is unable to retain it and complains that it feels tight. On examination, he has shortened fornices. What intervention is recommended?

options.C: temporarily discontinue the use of the prosthesis

explanation: The patient has a contracted socket. Causes of contracted sockets include radiation treatment, extrusion of enucleation implants, severe initial injury (alkali burns or extensive lacerations), poor surgical technique, multiple socket operations, and removal of the conformer or prosthesis for prolonged periods. Orbital implant exchange will not solve this issue and may cause more diﬃculty for the patient wearing the prosthesis. Discontinuance of prosthesis use is also counterproductive, because the fornix may further contract if the prosthesis is left out for an extended period of time. Temporary tarsorrhaphy also does not alter the forniceal contraction that has caused the problem. The best course of action in this case is forniceal reconstruction, usually with a mucosal graft (either buccal mucosa or contralateral conjunctiva). Stiﬀer graft with banked fascia, hard palate, ear cartilage, etc, may be used if signiﬁcant lower lid retraction is also present and will help with deepening of the fornix.

question: What systemic disease can lead to chronic dacryocystitis?
explanation: Chronic dacryocystitis occurs secondary to nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO). The most common cause of NLDO is idiopathic. However, a variety of inﬂammatory conditions can also cause NLDO and result in chronic dacryocystitis. The 2 most commonly seen entities in this regard are granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and sarcoidosis, both of which can involve the lacrimal drainage system, either primarily or secondarily, from the paranasal sinuses. If you answered this question in challenge mode, give yourself credit if you answered "sarcoid." While primary lacrimal sac tumors (typically squamous cell papillomas and carcinomas) may cause chronic dacryocystitis, malignant melanoma does not. Inﬂammatory conditions that aﬀect the mucous membranes, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and graft-versus- host disease, may cause loss of the punctum and/or canalicular obstruction, but they do not typically cause chronic dacryocystitis. &

question: In addition to the zygomatic, what bone makes up the lateral orbital wall?
explanation: The lateral wall of the orbit is composed of 2 bones: the zygomatic bone and the greater wing of the sphenoid. The lesser wing of the sphenoid encompasses the optic canal and is a part of the roof and medial orbital walls. The lacrimal bone is part of the medial wall, and the palatine bone is part of the ﬂoor. &

question: What organism is most commonly identiﬁed in necrotizing fasciitis?
explanation: Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus is the organism most commonly responsible for necrotizing fasciitis. Less commonly, a variety of other organisms, including aerobic and anaerobic gram- BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A 57-year-old woman with known metastatic uveal melanoma has developed a blind, painful eye. Treatments for the uveal melanoma have been exhausted and the vision is bare light perception. What is the best next step in management of this patient's condition?
explanation: Although the patient has a known metastasis, evisceration would not be the best option, given the risk of further local dissemination. Enucleation would allow for pain control as well as further histopathologic testing on the uveal melanoma. The use of retrobulbar lidocaine would provide transient pain control but is of limited long-term value. A Gunderson conjunctival ﬂap is beneﬁcial for ocular surface pain but would not allow for the pain BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: An external dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is an eﬀective treatment for what ﬁnding?
explanation: Dacryoliths often involve not only the canaliculi (causing chronic canaliculitis), but also the lacrimal sac. Lacrimal sac dacryoliths are often associated with nasolacrimal obstruction. A DCR would thus allow for removal of the lacrimal stones and re-establishment of lacrimal outﬂow. If a lacrimal sac tumor is suspected, a dacryocystectomy is indicated. If preoperative imaging shows tumor growth more inferiorly, then extirpation of the nasolacrimal duct should also be performed. In cases of lacrimal sac malignancy, a DCR is contraindicated, because there is a need to maintain the integrity of the lacrimal sac mucosa, to allow for complete tumor removal. Furthermore, an intact bony lacrimal sac BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: Orbital cellulitis in a 7-year-old patient most commonly arises from where?
explanation: Infectious orbital cellulitis is an infection posterior to the orbital septum. The vast majority of cases are caused by bacterial sinusitis. In a 7-year-old patient, the maxillary and frontal sinuses are underdeveloped. Therefore, orbital cellulitis is most likely to arise from the ethmoidal sinus. Other causative factors include the thinness of the BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What procedure should be used for the initial approach to the repair of symptomatic punctal ectropion with limited horizontal lid laxity?
explanation: Although thermal cautery of the conjunctiva can help to improve punctal ectropion, it is often not long-lasting and results in recurrence. A more permanent solution is the medial spindle procedure. This entails excision of the conjunctiva and retractors inferior to the puncta, with inverting sutures to correct the eyelid and punctal ectropion. If BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What is a modiﬁable risk factor for thyroid eye disease (TED)?
explanation: Development of thyroid eye disease (TED) is up to 7 times more likely for smokers than nonsmokers. Non-modiﬁable risk factors include female gender, Graves hyperthyroidism, and age group: 40-44 years and 60-64 years in women, and 45-49 years and 65-69 years in men. Obesity, alcohol consumption, and hypertension are not risk factors for TED.

question: Which orbital wall should not be removed to achieve orbital decompression?
explanation: The goal of orbital decompression is to create space within the orbit to allow enlarged muscles and orbital fat to expand into additional space to relieve pressure on the optic nerve and its blood supply, as well as to reduce proptosis. It is usually performed in patients with thyroid eye disease. Disruption of the roof of the orbit could lead to complications involving the anterior cranial fossa. 3675- 4446- 896c- 6a703982cf89) .

question: In non-Asians, where does the orbital septum of the upper eyelid fuse with the levator aponeurosis?

options.A: 2–5 mm above the superior tarsal border

explanation: In non-Asians, the orbital septum fuses with the levator aponeurosis 2– 5 mm above the superior tarsal border. The levator aponeurosis attaches to the tarsus at the inferior third of the tarsus. The fusion of the periosteum of the facial bones, the periorbita, and the orbital septum is the arcus marginalis. Whitnall ligament acts as a pulley for the force of the levator muscle and provides suspensory support for the upper eyelid and the superior orbital tissues.

question: Measuring eyelid excursion from extreme downgaze to extreme upgaze evaluates what aspect of eyelid function?
explanation: Measuring eyelid excursion from extreme downgaze to extreme upgaze is a method to evaluate levator function and is helpful in determining which surgical procedure may be most eﬀective for treatment of ptosis. Levator advancement is less eﬀective in patients with poor levator function. Lid lag refers to immobility or lagging of the upper eyelid in downgaze and may be associated with Graves orbitopathy. Lagophthalmos is the inability to close the eye completely. The degree of ptosis is judged from the interpalpebral measurement, not by measuring eyelid excursion. 6 Filter by 50 per p.

question: During patient evaluation, the ophthalmologist attempts to digitally elevate the margin of the lower eyelid to the superior corneal limbus with the eye in primary position. The inability to perform this maneuver suggests what diagnosis?
explanation: In cicatricial ectropion, there is a vertical shortage of the anterior lamella, preventing manual repositioning of the eyelid. Potential causes include thermal or chemical burns, mechanical or surgical trauma (tumor removal or blepharoplasty), chronic actinic sun damage, rosacea, atopic dermatitis, eczematous dermatitis, BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: Perineural invasion, bone destruction, and pain are associated with what lacrimal gland mass?
explanation: Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) is the most common malignant epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland. This highly malignant carcinoma may cause pain because of perineural invasion and bone destruction. The relatively rapid course, with a history of generally less than 1 year, and early onset of pain help diﬀerentiate ACC from pleomorphic adenoma, which is painless and characteristically exhibits progressive proptosis for more than a year. The tumor usually extends into the posterior orbit because of its capacity to inﬁltrate and its lack of true encapsulation. Most lacrimal gland masses represent nonspeciﬁc inﬂammation (dacryoadenitis). They present with acute inﬂammatory signs and usually respond to anti-inﬂammatory medication. They do not cause bony destruction or exhibit perineural invasion. The vast majority of orbital lymphoproliferative lesions are non- Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). The typical lymphoproliferative lesion presents as a gradually progressive, painless mass, resulting in proptosis, a visible periocular mass, or ptosis. These tumors are often located anteriorly in the orbit or beneath the conjunctiva, where they may show the typical salmon-patch appearance. Lymphoproliferative lesions, whether benign or malignant, usually mold to surrounding orbital structures rather than invade them; consequently, disturbances of extraocular motility or visual function are unusual.

question: A patient has a small, painless, pink, pedunculated mass on the lower lid shown in the image. The area does not have any ulceration or discharge. What management is appropriate in this case?

options.A: timolol ophthalmic gel 0.5% applied topically twice daily
options.B: cryotherapy or excision to eliminate the lesion and minimize the risk of viral spread
options.C: observation with spontaneous resolution in 2 weeks

explanation: Verruca vulgaris (papilloma) lesions are pink, pedunculated, or sessile masses caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV). They are usually asymptomatic and, because they are contagious, patients may have multiple lesions. The lesions may resolve spontaneously. Cryotherapy or excision may also eradicate the lesion and reduce the chance of spread.

question: Medial canthal reconstructions should be attached to what structure in order to maintain globe apposition?
explanation: Reconstruction of the medial canthus is challenging due to the presence of the lacrimal outﬂow apparatus and the need for proper 3-dimensional positioning of the medial canthal tendon. The reconstruction must include attachment to the posterior lacrimal crest to restore the proper posterior curvature of the lid and avoid poor globe apposition. Attachment to the anterior lacrimal crest or to the nasal bone would be too anterior and not restore the proper antero-posterior position. Care must be taken to avoid damage to the lacrimal sac.

question: What surgical approach is preferred for a suspected tumor in the lacrimal gland region?
explanation: For a tumor in the lacrimal gland region, an eyelid-crease incision provides excellent exposure and good cosmesis. The vertical eyelid-splitting incision would disrupt the eyelid anatomy more than is necessary to reach the lacrimal gland. A sub-brow incision will result in a visible scar. The swinging lower eyelid approach is better suited for inferior orbital masses.

question: What type of foreign body could be followed with observation and without surgery when located deep in the orbit?
explanation: Because a bullet enters the orbit at high velocity (and therefore high temperature), it may be considered a sterile foreign body. The projectile portion (as opposed to the casing) is typically made of an alloy containing a variety of metals, including copper, steel, aluminum, and bronze. This combination is usually (but not always) nonreactive in orbital soft tissue. It is reasonable to leave in place a bullet fragment that is deep in the orbit as long as it is not causing a compressive optic neuropathy. Copper often induces a signiﬁcant inﬂammatory reaction in the orbit and should be removed. Both copper and iron can also have a chronic toxic eﬀect on the eye: chalcosis and siderosis bulbi, respectively.

question: What is the principal drawback to using a dermis-fat graft for acquired anophthalmos in adults?
explanation: ! & # Dermis fat grafting is a useful method to restore volume in the anophthalmic socket. Dermis fat grafts may be implanted in the upper eyelid to ﬁll out the sulcus in patients with a deep superior sulcus. They may also be used with exposure or extrusion of an implant when a limited amount of conjunctiva remains in the socket. The graft increases the amount of net conjunctiva available as the conjunctiva re-epithelializes over the front surface of the dermis. The main disadvantage compared to a synthetic implant is the unpredictable resorption of the fat, with resultant inadequate volume. Dermis fat grafts have minimal extrusion or infection rates, and the donor site morbidity is not typically a signiﬁcant issue.

question: Why is a conformer placed in the fornices after a routine enucleation with orbital implant? &

options.B: to help retain the orbital implant in the socket

explanation: Preventing contracted fornices after enucleation includes preserving as much conjunctiva as possible and limiting dissection in the fornices. Placing extraocular muscles in their normal anatomical positions also minimizes shortening of the fornices. It is recommended that the patient wear a conformer in the immediate postoperative period to maintain soft-tissue anatomy and minimize conjunctival shortening. Conformers and prostheses should not be removed for periods greater than 24 hours. The prosthesis can be removed and cleaned, especially in the presence of infection, but should be replaced promptly after irrigation of the socket.

question: What structure is most easily damaged by surgical dissection in the superolateral conjunctival cul-de-sac?
explanation: The lacrimal sac ductules consist of 2 to 6 ductules that extend from the orbital lobe of the lacrimal gland, into the palpebral lobe, and join the palpebral lobe ducts. From there, 8 to 12 major palpebral lobe ductules drain into the lateral superior fornix cul- de-sac. They are located 4-5 mm above the superior margin of the upper tarsus. Therefore, dissection in this area can cause injury and, potentially, secondary dry eye. Whitnall ligament attaches laterally with septa transversing through the stroma of the lacrimal gland and attaches to the inner aspect of the lateral orbital wall. The horns of the levator aponeurosis diﬀer from Whitnall in that they lie more inferior and toward the canthi. The lateral horn inserts onto the lateral orbital tubercle, and it divides the lacrimal gland into orbital and palpebral lobes, attaching ﬁrmly to the orbital tubercle. The lacrimal artery lies within the stroma of the lacrimal gland and is unlikely to be injured during surgery within the conjunctival cul-de-sac.

question: An 8-year-old girl is being evaluated for precocious puberty and acromegaly. She also has hearing loss and has had multiple broken bones. During the examination, the ophthalmologist ﬁnds unilateral proptosis. What is the preferred initial imaging study to deﬁne the expected lesion? Whitnall ligament D.
explanation: Fibrous dysplasia is a developmental bone disorder where normal bone is replaced with ﬁbrous bone tissue involving one or multiple regions. It is best appreciated on computed tomography (CT), which shows characteristic hyperostotic bone. Despite the patient's young age, CT is the best initial imaging of choice for diagnosis. Fibrous dysplasia associated with cutaneous pigmentation and endocrine disorders is a condition known as Albright syndrome. Fibrous dysplasia is also associated with neuroﬁbromatosis type II. in lower lid retraction.

question: What clinical scenario is best for temporary (Quickert) sutures to correct lower lid entropion?

options.D: when a more deﬁnitive procedure cannot be performed

explanation: Quickert suture is indicated as a temporizing solution for involutional, acute spastic entropion, and when a more deﬁnitive procedure cannot be performed. Quickert suture, as the name implies, can be performed quickly, but a downside is entropion recurrence when the suture is used as the sole intervention. If the lower lid retractor complex is disinserted, retractor advancement surgery is required. Cicatricial entropion requires addressing the underlying cause and often requires a tarsal fracture operation (mild to moderate cicatricial changes) or a tarsal plate graft (severe cicatricial changes).

question: A 35-year-old patient presents with an acquired pigmented area involving the majority of the lower eyelid. The lesion has variable pigmentation and irregular borders. The ophthalmologist suspects possible melanoma because of a central area of elevation. What is the most appropriate initial course of action? &

options.A: observation for change in appearance or thickness
options.B: incisional biopsy to incorporate some nonpathologic tissue to demonstrate the transition area
options.D: incisional biopsy incorporating the maximum thickness of the lesion

explanation: The patient described has a presentation worrisome for malignant melanoma. It is important to biopsy the area of maximum thickness to determine if there is vertical invasion, and BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: What fat pad is traversed when performing a browpexy?
explanation: The retro-orbicularis oculi fat pad (ROOF) is suspended during a browpexy procedure. It is accessed through the upper eyelid incision during a blepharoplasty. Postseptal superior dissection is carried out to identify the ROOF. This fat pad is usually suspended with a 4-0 Vicryl suture to the frontal periosteum to achieve an internal brow ﬁxation/elevation. Medial preaponeurotic and central aponeurotic fat pads are located within the eyelid and do not achieve brow elevation when manipulated. The sub-orbicularis oculi fat pad is located within the lower eyelid.

question: While performing a medial wall decompression, an ophthalmologist encounters clear ﬂuid. The ophthalmologist suspects that it is cerebral spinal ﬂuid. Identiﬁcation of, and staying inferior to, what landmark could have minimized the chance of this complication?
explanation: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries pass through the corresponding ethmoidal foramina in the medial orbital wall along the frontoethmoidal suture. This suture represents the level of the cribriform plate, the ﬂoor of the anterior cranial fossa. Trauma above this ethmoidal foramina can cause inadvertent entry into the cranial vault and subsequent cerebral spinal ﬂuid (CSF) rhinorrhea. The trochlea is located along the orbital roof and if penetrated can cause CSF rhinorrhea. However, it is unlikely to be involved during a medial wall decompression. The medial rectus muscle belly is not a landmark, as it would not allow for suﬃcient decompression to take place. Similarly, the lacrimal crest is a vertically oriented landmark that is too anterior to the plane of dissection during a medial wall decompression. 72a7- 450c- bcd9- 936cdf7f78cb) .

question: What are the primary contributing factors in the development of involutional entropion of the lower eyelid?

options.A: horizontal laxity, disinsertion of lower eyelid retractors, and orbicularis override
options.B: vertical laxity, tarsal conjunctival scarring, and orbicularis weakness
options.C: horizontal laxity, tarsal conjunctival scarring, and orbicularis override
options.D: horizontal laxity, disinsertion of lower eyelid retractors, and orbicularis weakness

explanation: Involutional entropion is primarily due to horizontal laxity and vertical instability, owing to disinsertion of the lower lid retractors. Orbicularis override is also a common feature, either due to soft tissue laxity or secondary to a spastic component. Keratopathy from entropion leads to a secondary orbicularis spasm as a protective measure for the cornea. However, because of the horizontal and vertical instability, the preseptal tarsus BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: For an infant with congenital anophthalmos, what additional clinical feature might an ophthalmologist expect to ﬁnd?

options.D: increased horizontal and vertical palpebral ﬁssure distances

explanation: Congenital anophthalmia often results in poor orbital growth. It appears that a normal globe is necessary to stimulate growth of the surrounding orbital bones, and lack of a globe in infants or very young children results in signiﬁcant facial asymmetry. Maxillary hypoplasia may also occur. Patients with anophthalmia typically have horizontal and vertical shortening of their palpebral ﬁssures. Microphthalmia with or without cyst is a separate entity and not true anophthalmia, but can also result in a hypoplastic orbit. A variety of maneuvers may help to stimulate orbital growth in cases of congenital anophthalmia, including progressively larger conformers, tissue expanders placed in the orbit, and dermis fat grafts, which have been shown to grow with the child.

question: What is the most common cause of pseudoptosis?
explanation: The most common cause of pseudoptosis is dermatochalasis, which is redundant upper eyelid skin that hangs over the lashes and reduces the margin-reﬂex distance. Brow ptosis and enophthalmos can also cause reduction in the margin-reﬂex distance, but are not as common as dermatochalasis. Graves disease typically causes lid retraction, not ptosis.

question: The patient in the ﬁgure is unhappy with his facial appearance. What surgical approach could be used to improve his appearance around his eyes?
explanation: Along with dermatochalasis and prominent lower lid fat pads, the ﬁgure shows involutional skin changes and descent and deﬂation of the midface. When approaching the lower lid, the continuum between the lower lid and the cheek must be addressed together. SOOF is suborbicularis oculi fat found posterior to the orbicularis muscle and attached superiorly at the arcus marginalis. Midface rejuvenation involves SOOF and midface elevation, combined with midface inﬂation and lower lid fat sculpting. A preperiosteal SOOF lift can create midface rejuvenation as well as correct mild to moderate lower eyelid ectropion/retraction when there is anterior lamellar skin shortage. The midface is accessed either transconjunctivally, subciliary, or from the temporal scalp. The SOOF is observed as dark-yellow fat on the anterior surface of the maxilla beneath the orbicularis oculi. The SOOF is then dissected from the underlying periosteum, then lifted and sutured to the arcus marginalis. In addition to preperiosteal midface lifting, a subperiosteal approach can also be used to elevate the midface. Finally, fat transfer or injectable ﬁllers can be utilized to sculpt the midface as a means to reinﬂate the soft tissue. A subperiosteal midface lift can also be used for facial rejuvenation as well as for cases of severe lower eyelid retraction, which is not seen in the ﬁgure. The subperiosteal midface can be accessed through the lateral canthus, superior gingival sulcus, or temporal scalp incision. The periosteum is incised 3 mm inferior to the orbital rim, and a periosteal elevator is used to undermine the midface/maxilla/zygoma periosteum. The mobilized midface is then sutured to the arcus marginalis medially and temporalis fascia laterally. Lower facelift will improve the nasolabial folds, jowls, and neck but will not help with the area around his eyes. Platysmaplasty can correct troublesome platysmal bands within the neck. The neck is not BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: The optic canal traverses which orbital bone?
explanation: The optic canal is 8-10 mm long and is located within the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone. The ethmoid, maxillary, and palatine bones are also components of the orbit, but they are not part of the optic canal.

question: The lacrimal sac sits proximate to what nasal structure?
explanation: The lacrimal fossa and lacrimal bone are located just anterior to the insertion of the middle turbinate. When viewing the lacrimal sac at an intranasal perspective, the lacrimal sac corresponds to BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: A patient has a unilateral supraduction deﬁcit and positive forced ductions. He also has upper eyelid retraction. What is the most likely etiology?
explanation: Graves ophthalmopathy is the most common cause of eyelid retraction (and eyelid retraction is the most common clinical feature of Graves ophthalmopathy). Neither third nerve palsy nor orbital trauma would produce eyelid retraction. Although progressive supranuclear palsy, orbital trauma, and third cranial nerve palsy are conceivable etiologies for a supraduction deﬁcit, only orbital trauma and Graves ophthalmopathy would have positive forced ductions. Positive forced ductions indicate a restrictive extraocular muscle problem and can be found in traumatic orbital fracture with entrapment of the inferior rectus or surrounding connective tissue, Graves disease, postsurgical strabismus, and Brown syndrome in the adducting position.

question: An 8-year-old presents with rapid onset of unilateral proptosis. Imaging demonstrates an enhancing orbital mass. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: urgent incisional biopsy with map biopsy of the conjunctiva to assess for pagetoid spread
options.B: urgent incisional biopsy coordinated with the pediatric service for possible intraoperative bone marrow biopsy and lumbar puncture
options.C: high-dose steroids and repeat imaging in 3 weeks
options.D: urgent initiation of systemic chemotherapy and orbital radiation

explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary orbital malignancy in childhood and a life-threatening condition that progresses rapidly. Biopsy should be performed immediately, and it is helpful in suspected cases to obtain a bone marrow biopsy and a lumbar puncture while the patient is under general anesthesia. Depending on the results of systemic workup, additional resection of the tumor may not be necessary. Complete excision is often diﬃcult. High-dose steroids and repeat imaging in 3 weeks would be a very poor choice, with expected progression of the disease during the delay in treatment. The mainstay of treatment once the diagnosis is conﬁrmed is systemic evaluation for metastasis, followed by chemotherapy and radiation. Map biopsies and pagetoid spread are seen in sebaceous carcinoma and not in rhabdomyosarcoma.

question: The mucocutaneous junction represents an important demarcation of the ocular surface. In a normal eye, the mucocutaneous junction colocalizes with what portion of the lid margin?

options.A: anterior to the meibomian gland oriﬁces
options.B: posterior to the meibomian gland oriﬁces
options.D: between the meibomian gland oriﬁces and the lash follicle

explanation: The mucocutaneous junction of the eyelid margin is often confused with the gray line. The gray line is a section of pretarsal orbicularis (Riolan) muscle just anterior to the tarsus. The mucocutaneous junction is located posterior to the meibomian gland oriﬁces on the eyelid margin.

question: What structure(s) most closely co-localize with the axial position of the cribriform plate? &

options.A: superior border of the cartilaginous nasal septum

explanation: The skull base, which separates the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses from the intracranial cavity, is composed of the cribriform plate (roof of the nasal cavity) and the fovea ethmoidalis (roof of the ethmoid air cells). The boundary between these 2 structures is the root of the middle turbinate. The axial level of the skull base is best approximated by the frontoethmoidal suture and the 2 (anterior and posterior) ethmoidal foramina found along the medial orbital wall. The medial canthal tendon lies well below (7-10 mm) this level. The cartilaginous portion of the nasal septum is also found below and anterior to the skull base; the roof of the BCSC Excerpt References Notes.

question: Optociliary shunt vessels are a feature of what entity?
explanation: Orbital meningiomas originate in the arachnoid of the optic nerve sheath. They most commonly occur in women in their third and fourth decades of life. Symptoms include gradual, painless, unilateral loss of vision. Examination ﬁndings may include decreased visual acuity; relative aﬀerent pupillary defect; proptosis; ophthalmoplegia; normal, atrophic, or swollen optic nerve head; and visible optociliary shunt vessels (also identiﬁed as "tortuous vessels"). Orbital cavernous hemangiomas also occur more commonly in women. They are the most common benign neoplasm of the orbit. Findings include progressive proptosis, retinal striae, hyperopia, optic nerve compression, increased intraocular pressure, and strabismus. Orbital ﬁbrous dysplasia is a benign developmental disorder of bone. Computed tomography (CT) shows hyperostotic bone. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows lack of dural enhancement, which distinguishes ﬁbrous dysplasia from meningioma.

question: A 50-year-old man complains of a droopy left lid that seems to have gradually worsened. He reports a previous history of rigid gas-permeable (RGP) contact lens wear. What is the most likely etiology of his ptosis and the associated examination ﬁndings?

options.B: neurogenic - associated with motility abnormality limiting left eye adduction, supraduction, and infraduction

question: Increased risk and severity of thyroid eye disease in patients with Graves hyperthyroidism are more likely in what group of patients?

options.A: patients with a high serum T4 level
options.B: patients in their 3rd decade of life

explanation: Thyroid eye disease (TED) disease is 6 times more common in women than in men. Peak incidence rates occur in age groups 40 to 44 years and 60 to 64 years in women, and 45 to 49 years and 65 to 69 years in men. Smoking is associated with increased risk and severity of TED. Patients can be hypothyroid, euthyroid, or hyperthyroid. Severity of TED usually does not parallel serum levels of T or T . question: Biopsy of a lacrimal gland mass via the palpebral lobe of the lacrimal gland risks damage to what structure?
explanation: The lacrimal gland is divided into orbital and palpebral lobes by indentation from the lateral horn of the levator aponeurosis. Lacrimal excretory ducts pass through the palpebral portion of the gland, so removal of, or damage to (by biopsy), the palpebral portion of the gland can severely reduce secretion from the lacrimal gland. The accessory lacrimal glands are located in the superior fornix (Krauss) and superior border of the tarsus (Wolfring). The origin of the lacrimal artery is the ophthalmic artery, which is not near the palpebral lobe. The eﬀerent nerve supply to the lacrimal gland is by way of parasympathetic ﬁbers from cranial nerve VII in the greater superﬁcial petrosal nerve, which sends ﬁbers to the sphenopalatine ganglion, and then by way of the zygomatic nerve.

question: What are the mucin-secreting cells of the conjunctival fornices?
explanation: Goblet cells are the mucin-secreting cells of the conjunctiva and are located in the fornices. The glands of Krause and Wolfring are accessory lacrimal glands found in the subconjunctival tissue, mainly in the upper and lower eyelids. The glands of Wolfring are found primarily along the nonmarginal tarsal borders, and the glands of Krause are found in the fornices. The meibomian glands are sebaceous glands located within the tarsal plate.

question: While playing baseball, a 22- year-old man was struck in the right eye with a ball. His visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes. Intraocular pressure and fundus examinations are normal. A computed tomography (CT) scan shows a fracture of the right socket that extends to approximately two-thirds of the orbital ﬂoor. What is the most likely clinical ﬁnding?
explanation: The clinical scenario presented is a right orbital ﬂoor fracture. The infraorbital groove and infraorbital canal, which transmit the infraorbital artery and the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, travel along the orbital ﬂoor and can be injured. Clinically, patients are likely to present with cranial nerve (CN) V hypoesthesia that is typically transient. Epistaxis is more likely to occur after medial wall fracture or trauma. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid rhinorrhea is likely to occur after an orbital roof fracture. Diplopia following a ﬂoor fracture is more likely to occur in the vertical orientation rather than horizontally. 2 dermatochalasis.

question: A 35-year-old woman with drooping upper eyelid skin associated with recurrent swelling has what condition?
explanation: Blepharochalasis is a rare familial variant of angioneurotic edema. It typically occurs in younger persons, most commonly young females, and is characterized by idiopathic episodes of inﬂammatory edema of the eyelids. As a result of recurrent bouts of inﬂammation and edema, the eyelid skin of a patient with blepharochalasis becomes thin and wrinkled, simulating the appearance of dermatochalasis. In addition, true ptosis, herniation of the orbital lobe of the lacrimal gland, atrophy of the orbital fat pads, and prominent eyelid vascularity may be associated with blepharochalasis. Surgical repair of the eyelid- skin changes and the ptosis that result from blepharochalasis may be complicated by repeated episodes of inﬂammation and edema, causing recurrence of the ptosis and other eyelid changes. Dermatochalasis refers to redundancy of eyelid skin and is often associated with orbital fat prolapse. Benign essential blepharospasm (BEB) is a bilateral focal dystonia that is characterized by increased blinking and involuntary spasms of the periocular protractor muscles. Meige syndrome is a lower facial dystonia associated with BEB. ethmoidal foramina.

question: The patient below presents after recently immigrating from South America. A complete examination is performed and is normal other than the ﬁndings shown in the image. What is the appropriate recommendation with regard to follow-up for this patient?

explanation: The patient exhibits the typical slate-grey pigmentation of the skin and sclera seen in oculodermal melanocytosis (OM, nevus of Ota). Note the distribution along the maxillary division (V ) of the trigeminal nerve. OM is more prevalent in Asian, African, and Hispanic populations. OM is a congenital lesion, in contradistinction to primary acquired melanosis (PAM), an acquired condition of older white populations. Unlike PAM, which may progress to skin melanoma, patients with OM are at risk for choroidal (0.25%) and meningeal melanoma. Routine screening by dilated fundus examination may be diﬃcult: Patients with OM have a thickened uvea, and as a result have poor pupillary dilation. B-scan ultrasonography may be necessary to deﬁnitively rule out an intraocular mass. question: A 15-year-old patient has chronic tearing from the right eye. Probing on the right reveals a soft stop through the lower punctum and a hard stop through the upper punctum. What is the most likely site of obstruction?
explanation: "Soft stop" is a term used to indicate a soft tissue obstruction palpated within the upper lacrimal drainage system during probing. A "hard stop" is palpated with the tip of a Bowman probe when successful probing has been performed through the canaliculus, common canaliculus, and into the lacrimal sac; palpation of the bony lacrimal sac fossa along the medial wall of the lacrimal sac feels "hard." In contrast, a soft tissue obstruction anywhere along this course will feel "soft." In this case, the hard stop palpated through the upper canaliculus indicates patency of both the upper canaliculus and common canaliculus. Therefore, the lower canaliculus is obstructed. Probing of the nasolacrimal duct may also show an obstruction, but because of the surrounding bony duct, diﬀerentiation between a soft stop and hard stop is more diﬃcult.

question: What produces the majority of the lipid layer of the precorneal tear ﬁlm? lower canaliculus B. 64 Correct Answer lower nasolacrimal duct C.
explanation: The tear ﬁlm comprises 3 layers: the lipid layer (anterior), aqueous layer, and mucin layer (posterior). The lipid layer is secreted by the meibomian glands, and to a lesser extent, the glands of Zeis. The aqueous layer is secreted from the lacrimal glands. question: What brow lift procedure is used for treatment of mild brow ptosis and is performed through an upper eyelid blepharoplasty incision?
explanation: Browpexy treats mild brow ptosis and is performed through an upper eyelid blepharoplasty incision. During a browpexy procedure, the tissues below the brow are resuspended with sutures to the frontal bone periosteum above the orbital rim. Larger amounts of brow ptosis can be treated with a direct brow elevation, performed with incisions placed at the upper edge of the brow hairs; endoscopic brow and forehead lift, performed through small incisions approximately 1cm behind the hairline; or a pretrichial brow and forehead lift, performed through an incision just below the hairline.

question: What causes acute spastic entropion?
explanation: Acute spastic entropion is caused by ocular irritation or inﬂammation. Disinsertion of eyelid retractors and horizontal eyelid laxity contribute to involutional entropion. Deﬁciency of eyelid skin is a cause of cicatricial ectropion.

question: What is a contraindication to evisceration?
explanation: The potential for sympathetic ophthalmia is a common admonition against evisceration and for enucleation. In fact, sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare event, and no deﬁnitive correlation with evisceration has been proved (although some anecdotal evidence does exist). The most ominous risk of evisceration is an occult intraocular malignancy; evisceration would allow spillage of tumor out of the eye. Because of this possibility, evisceration should not be performed without a detailed view of the fundus.

question: What is the most common presentation of rhabdomyosarcoma?
explanation: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary orbital malignancy of childhood. The average age of onset is 5–7 years. The classic clinical picture is that of a child with sudden onset and rapid progression of unilateral proptosis. However, patients in their early teens may experience a less dramatic course, with gradually progressive proptosis developing over weeks to more than a month. There is often a marked adnexal response with edema and discoloration of the eyelids. Ptosis and strabismus may also be present. A mass may be palpable, particularly in the superonasal quadrant of the eyelid, and it may cause proptosis if suﬃciently large. However, the tumor may be retrobulbar, may involve any quadrant of the orbit, and may in rare cases arise from the conjunctiva. Although pain is an occasional complaint, it is seen in only a minority of rhabdomyosarcoma cases. Optic neuropathy is uncommon in rhabdomyosarcoma unless the tumor is allowed to progress without timely diagnosis and treatment.

question: A 54-year-old woman presented with pain, including left-eye enophthalmos and diplopia. Imaging revealed the following lesion with inﬁltration of the left orbit (see ﬁgures). What past medical history would be helpful in making the diagnosis?

options.B: travel to the Ohio River Valley

explanation: Although virtually any cancer of the internal organs, hematopoietic system, or skin can metastasize to the orbit, most orbital metastases derive from lung, breast, and prostate tumors. The presence of pain, proptosis, inﬂammation, bone destruction, and early ophthalmoplegia suggests the possibility of metastatic carcinoma. Some 75% of patients have a history of a known primary tumor, but orbital metastasis is the presenting sign of cancer in 25% of patients. The extraocular muscles are frequently involved because of their abundant blood supply. The second most common site is the bone marrow space of the sphenoid bone because of the relatively high volume of low-ﬂow blood in this area. Lytic destruction of this part of the lateral orbital wall is highly suggestive of metastatic disease. Elevation of serum carcinoembryonic antigen levels also may suggest a metastatic process. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy can be performed in the oﬃce and may obviate the need for orbitotomy and open biopsy.

question: A patient presents following Mohs surgery with a lower eyelid defect greater than 60 . What is the best technique to repair this large lower eyelid defect?

options.A: free tarsal graft from upper eyelid and full-thickness skin graft
options.B: tarsoconjunctival ﬂap from upper eyelid with full-thickness skin graft
options.C: direct primary closure of the lower eyelid

explanation: The most appropriate technique to perform in the situation described is a tarsoconjunctival ﬂap from upper eyelid with full- thickness skin graft. This procedure allows for the reconstruction of the posterior and anterior lamella without violating the principle of placing 2 grafts (eg, free tarsal graft from upper eyelid and full-thickness skin graft) adjacent to one another. Rotational or primary direct closure is not amenable in defects greater than 50%.

question: A 57-year-old patient was recently diagnosed with a low- grade isolated orbital lymphoma. What is the preferred treatment? tarsoconjunctival ﬂap from upper eyelid with full-thickness skin graft B. 82 Correct Answer direct primary closure of the lower eyelid C.
explanation: The most common type of orbital lymphoma is extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma, which is a low-grade malignancy. The typical treatment is external beam radiotherapy, with 10-year survival rates of 92%. A surgical cure usually is not possible because of the inﬁltrative nature of lymphoid tumors. Corticosteroids can decrease the size of an orbital lymphoma but are not adequate treatment. Chemotherapy such as carboplatin sometimes is used in cases of systemic lymphoma. iris nevi or melanoma.

question: Plexiform neuroﬁbromas are most commonly associated with what ocular disorder?
explanation: Plexiform neuroﬁbroma can lead to secondary glaucoma. Plexiform neuroﬁbroma stems from a proliferation of Schwann cells and can present with neuroﬁbromatosis type 1 (NF1, also known as von Recklinghausen disease). The upper eyelid and orbit are usually aﬀected, and neuroﬁbromas can directly inﬁltrate the angle. A subretinal osteoma is generally a benign, ossifying tumor in which the choroid is replaced by bone. It is not associated with NF-1 but is rather a sporadic disease with no known risk factors. A choroidal melanoma is a malignant neoplasm of the choroid and is usually sporadic without association with NF-1. Iris nevi or iris melanoma are also not related to NF-1.

question: What structure of the upper eyelid is analogous to a component in the lower eyelid retractors?
explanation: The lower eyelid anatomy may be considered a simpliﬁed or primitive analog of the upper lid. In the lower lid, 2 retractors are present: the capsulopalpebral fascia and the inferior tarsal muscle. Because both of these structures are rudimentary and essentially inseparable surgically, they are usually coupled together as the "lower lid retractors." The capsulopalpebral fascia component of the lower lid retractors is analogous to the levator aponeurosis of the upper lid. question: What method is typically used to repair a large lower eyelid defect involving more than 50 of the eyelid?
explanation: The eyelid-sharing technique of a Hughes ﬂap combined with skin grafting of the anterior lamella would be an ideal repair technique for a large defect of the lower eyelid. Note that repair of a large full-thickness eyelid defect requires reconstruction of the mucosa-lined posterior lamella and the cutaneous anterior lamella. At least one of the lamellae should be a vascularized ﬂap; free grafts of both lamellae will not survive. Thus another option in this case would be a free tarsoconjunctival graft from the contralateral upper eyelid with vascular supply from a pedicled skin–muscle ﬂap. The Cutler-Beard procedure is an eyelid-sharing technique in which a full-thickness lower eyelid ﬂap is moved into the defect of the upper eyelid by advancement of the ﬂap behind the remaining lower eyelid margin. Primary closure of a large defect involving more than 50% of the lower lid is unlikely to be possible, and granulation alone would lead to a poor functional and cosmetic result.
